title: Flow surge bench diary (mini sweep): korey
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal log of a short, targeted benchmark sweep to understand how short-duration surge arrivals interact with prefix/KV cache priming and small-batch multiplexing on the 13B quantized tier. Trying to capture actionable knobs for canary autoscale policies.

Hypotheses going in:
- Very short bursts (500ms - 3s) will hurt p99 more than p95, because warmup + GPU kernel churn + queueing create long tails.
- Prefix/KV cache hits will cut p95 by 20-40% in most cases, but p99 improvements depend on whether the cold requests hit hotpath evictions.
- Small multiplexing (batch size 2-4) with constant timeout (10ms) reduces tail by smoothing microburst serialization but can increase median if timeout triggers unnecessarily.

Setup summary (mini-sweep):
- Model: open-instruct-13b-8k-qat (int8-ish, standard runtime kernels for amp-int8)
- HW: node group A: 1x A100-40GB, node group B: 2x T4 (control)
- Serving config: single-model variant, dynamic batching enabled, multiplexing layer toggled per-run
- Clients: 50 concurrent connections across 3 client hosts (emulated real traffic), Poisson arrival with configurable burst factor
- Request profile: prompt length 80 tokens, generation 150 tokens expected (streaming enabled), small response chunking (approx 32 tokens per chunk)
- KV cache priming: three variants tested: cold (no priming), shared-prefix primed (same prefix pre-warmed by synthetic shadow traffic), per-tenant primed (per-connection prefix warm)
- Runs: each config ran 10x 120s trials; recorded per-request latencies, p50/p90/p95/p99, QPS, GPU utilization, batch size distribution, and number of context-switch evictions

Representative results (condensed):
1) Baseline: cold cache, no multiplexing, A100
- avg QPS: 68
- p50: 18ms
- p90: 62ms
- p95: 120ms
- p99: 420ms (heavy tail)
- GPU util: 68% (lots of short idle gaps)
- notes: many long tails coincide with kernel-loading events and small bursts queuing for single GPU worker threads

2) Shared-prefix primed, no multiplexing, A100
- avg QPS: 76
- p50: 16ms
- p90: 48ms
- p95: 82ms
- p99: 240ms
- GPU util: 74%
- notes: clear win on p95, p99 improved but still pronounced. Memory evictions recorded in 7% of requests that hit long tails.

3) Shared-prefix + multiplexing (batch timeout 10ms, max-batch 4), A100
- avg QPS: 81
- p50: 18ms
- p90: 45ms
- p95: 68ms
- p99: 160ms
- GPU util: 82%
- notes: best tail behavior overall; multiplexing smoothed short bursts and allowed more efficient kernel/pipelining. Median slightly worse vs primed-only but acceptable.

4) Per-tenant primed + multiplexing, A100
- avg QPS: 78
- p50: 15ms
- p90: 44ms
- p95: 64ms
- p99: 150ms
- GPU util: 80%
- notes: per-tenant priming marginally better than shared for p50/p95; suggests per-tenant locality matters when requests include small differing prefixes.

5) Cold cache + multiplexing (same params), A100
- avg QPS: 72
- p50: 19ms
- p90: 54ms
- p95: 110ms
- p99: 330ms
- notes: multiplexing alone reduces some queuing but cannot substitute for priming; kernel cold-starts still dominant tail source.

6) Baseline runs on T4 (for context/cost): cold cache, no multiplexing
- avg QPS: 28
- p50: 35ms
- p90: 120ms
- p95: 260ms
- p99: 980ms
- GPU util: 45% (starved by kernel latency)
- notes: T4 clearly worse for bursty latency-sensitive traffic; not a candidate for low-latency tiers.

Quick syntheses / takeaways:
- KV/prefix priming is the single most effective lever for improving p95 and p99 on short surges. Invest in cheap shadow-priming for hot routes (pre-warm on deploy/scale event).
- Small multiplexing (timeout ~10ms, max-batch 4) is a good default for smoothing microbursts without materially harming median latency; tune timeouts per route.
- Tuning can be route-specific: streaming chat routes with many small outputs benefit more from multiplexing + priming than single-shot long-completion routes.
- For autoscale policy triggers: consider combining QPS slope + fraction of long-tail requests (p99 > X ms) rather than raw concurrent connections. This prevents oscillation on short bursts.

Observed anomalies to investigate:
- 11/03 trial sequence 4 showed an unexplained cluster of p99 spikes even with per-tenant priming; correlated with high kernel load on host and a concurrent gitlab CI job that pinned GPU memory. Need to reproduce with isolation.
- Some p99s align with batch-size 1 processing where the worker had just finished a larger batch; investigate worker dispatch fairness.

Action items (next quick experiments):
- Re-run targeted isolation test: reproduce sequence 4 anomaly on a dedicated, clean node (no CI interference). (owner: Korey, due: 11/10)
- Sweep multiplex timeout 6/10/20ms on primed/shared/per-tenant combinations; collect batch-size histograms (owner: Maya, due: 11/12)
- Try tiny early-ack strategy (respond with first chunk faster) vs standard chunking to see tail impact for streaming consumers (owner: Ravi, due: 11/14)
- Add lightweight telemetry to annotate long-tail traces with kernel-load and eviction counts for later correlation (owner: Korey + SRE)

Notes to self:
- Keep these runs short (120s) — they are cheap and capture microburst behavior; but longer runs (10m) needed to validate steady-state for autoscale configs.
- For canary, enable shared-prefix priming for top 10 routes and set multiplex timeout to 10ms; monitor p99 delta over first 24h.

Raw snippets and mental model (for future doc):
- Think of bursts as two-phase: microburst arrival (0-3s) dominated by kernel loading and queueing; sustained phase (>10s) dominated by batch efficiency. Different levers for each.
- Decision table (very rough):
  * microburst: priming + short multiplexing; favor warm nodes; avoid low-end T4 lanes
  * sustained high qps: larger batch sizes + static pre-quantized kernels; optimize for throughput/cost

Random quick logs:
- trial 7 (primed+multx): batch size distribution: [1: 12%, 2: 34%, 3: 28%, 4: 26%]
- trial 2 (cold baseline): eviction_count >0 for 7% of requests; these map to p99 bucket

If I get time: make a tiny viz (sparkline) and drop into #perf-bench. For now, this is the scratch diary.
